segments.text: Let me begin with a question that sounds simple and then gets complicated very quickly.
What does it mean to be anti-racist?
And before anyone answers, it means not being racist.
That answer is worth examining.
Not because it is always wrong, but because it may be incomplete.
We are going to talk about racism as a personal experience, but also as something that can
be carried through institutions, policies, procedures, habits, and assumptions.
We are going to talk about anti-racism and what it asks of people who work inside institutions
that serve the public.
We are also going to talk about DEI, diversity, equity, and inclusion, without treating the
acronym as a magic word.
Some DEI programs are thoughtful.
Some are shallow.
Some are poorly evaluated.
Some practices may raise real legal or ethical concerns.
And some public attacks on DEI rely on claims that simply do not survive contact with evidence.
That distinction matters.
A serious conversation can defend the goal of fair, effective public service while criticizing
a training that is embarrassing, a metric that is vague, or a program that cannot show
what changed.
And we should say at the outset that this is not a conversation about assigning inherited
guilt.
People born today did not personally choose slavery, segregation, redlining, exclusionary
immigration laws, or every institutional decision that came before them.
But people today do inherit institutions.
We inherit their rules, their data, their buildings, their budgets, their traditions,
and sometimes their blind spots.
The question is not whether we should feel guilty for history.
The question is what responsibility comes with operating the systems we have received.
Especially when those systems are public, a government office is not merely a workplace.
It is a place where someone applies for a benefit, reports a problem, seeks protection, pays a
fee, finds housing, gets an identification document, or asks whether the law will work
for them too.
So the stakes are practical.
Who gets through the door?
Who can understand the form?
Who is believed?
Who waits longer?
Who gets a second chance to correct an error?
Who is represented in the workforce, and who has influence over the decisions?
We are going to take those questions seriously.
But we are also going to keep them human.
This should sound like two colleagues thinking aloud, not two people reading a compliance
memo.
Let's start with the language.
What do we mean when we say racism?
At the most familiar level, racism can involve racial prejudice, stereotyping, hostility,
discrimination, or unequal treatment between people.
Someone uses a slur, a supervisor makes a racial joke, a landlord refuses an applicant
because of race, a hiring manager decides that a black candidate is not a culture fit while
accepting the same ambiguity from a white candidate.
Those examples are recognizable because we can see an individual actor.
There is a person, a choice, and often a direct statement.
But if we define racism only as an obviously hateful individual, we miss a large part of
how unequal outcomes are produced.
Students operate through eligibility rules, funding choices schedules, forms, software
location, language, staffing, professional norms, and discretion.
Those systems can create unequal effects even when no one person announces an intention to
harm.
Let's make that concrete.
Suppose a public agency says, everyone can access this service online.
That sounds equal.
But the website does not work with a screen reader.
The instructions are written at a level many people cannot easily understand.
Key information is only in English.
The application assumes stable broadband, a printer, paid time off, and a bank account.
The helpline closes at four.
The rule is the same on paper.
The opportunity is not the same in practice.
And that is where a phrase like sameness is not always fairness can be useful as long
as we do not use it as a shortcut.
We still have to investigate.
We still have to ask what is causing the gap.
We do not get to declare that every disparity proves racial intent.
Exactly.
A disparity is a signal, not a full explanation.
Race may be part of the story.
So may income, geography, disability, age, language, transportation, immigration status,
family responsibilities, or prior contact with government.
These factors can overlap and they can compound one another.
So does acknowledging structural racism mean reducing every problem to race?
No.
In fact, good equity analysis should make the question more rigorous.
It should lead to better data, better interviews, better comparison groups, better measurement,
and greater humility about what we do not know.
That humility is important because people often hear the word structural and imagine
a claim that every outcome was planned by a committee.
But a structure does not require a conspiracy.
A structure can be an accumulated set of decisions that interact over time.
And that is not an argument for blaming one employee at a desk.
It is an argument for tracing how decisions travel.
Who set the rules?
What data informed them?
What assumptions got treated as neutral?
Who had the power to challenge them?
This is why intent and impact have to be held together.
Intent matters.
It matters morally, legally, and relationally.
But intent is not a substitute for examining consequences.
If a public program repeatedly fails a group of residents, we meant well is not a performance
measure.
So perhaps the first working definition is this.
Racism can be an individual act, a patterned practice, or a system of rules and conditions
that assigns different risks, opportunities, credibility, or access along racial lines.
Yes.
With one addition, the definition should invite investigation rather than close it.
The point is not to label every imperfect result.
The point is to understand what is happening well enough to change an unfair result when
the evidence shows one.
Which brings us to anti-racism.
If it is not simply the absence of a racist feeling, what is it?
I would describe anti-racism as the deliberate practice of identifying, challenging, preventing,
and changing racial inequities in relationships, organizations, and systems.
The word deliberate does a lot of work.
Think about workplace safety.
An organization does not say we are not pro-accident, so we are finished.
It identifies hazards, collects information, trains people, changes procedures, investigates
failures, and monitors whether the change is helped.
Anti-racism works similarly.
It asks, where might unequal treatment or unequal access be built into the way we recruit,
decide, communicate, enforce, purchase, inspect, or deliver?
What does the data show?
What does the data not show?
Who has been missing from the design process?
And that is different from a purity test.
A purity test asks, did you say the perfect thing?
Are you one of the good people?
A practice asks, what happened?
Who was affected?
What can we learn?
What will we change?
And how will we know if it worked?
This matters because the public debate often turns anti-racism into a question of personal
identity.
Are you racist or not racist?
Are you for DEI or against DEI?
Those binaries are emotionally efficient, but operationally useless.
They also encourage defensiveness.
If acknowledging a problem is treated as admitting you are a bad person, people will spend the
meeting proving that no problem exists.
There is a different way to frame responsibility.
We can say you may not have created the conditions you inherited, but you do have
choices about whether to reproduce them, study them, or change them.
That also makes room for people who are not racial equity specialists.
A front desk worker can notice that a form confuses residents.
A case manager can see that people with limited English are returning three times.
A manager can compare who receives overtime, stretch assignments, or corrective action.
A policy analyst can ask whether a rule is solving the problem it was created to solve.
One of those people needs to make a grand statement about American history before improving
a process.
A good anti-racist process also distinguishes between different kinds of claims.
One claim is legal.
Did the institution violate a statute, regulation, court order, or policy?
Another is empirical.
Are outcomes different and why?
Another is ethical.
Is the process fair or dignifying?
Another is managerial.
Is the program working?
Those questions overlap, but they are not identical.
That distinction is a guardrail.
A disparity is not automatically proof of illegal discrimination.
An action can be legal and still worth improving.
A well-intended program can be ineffective.
A practice can be lawful but demeaning.
We need enough language to tell those things apart.
And we need enough courage to act before we have perfect certainty.
If a public office sees that one group is waiting months longer, the responsible response
is not to freeze until every causal question is resolved.
It is to investigate, reduce avoidable harm, and keep learning.
That is the practical heart of anti-racism.
Attention plus action plus accountability.
Attention to patterns.
Action on barriers.
Accountability for whether the change made a difference.
And a willingness to revise the work.
Anti-racism should not be a performance of certainty.
It should be a disciplined refusal to accept preventable inequity as normal.
Let's turn to the myths, because a lot of the public argument happens there.
What are people being told DEI means?
Let's take the first myth.
Anti-racism means white people are bad.
No.
It is possible to discuss racial inequality without declaring that every white person
is individually responsible for creating it.
It is also possible to say that white people can benefit from institutional patterns they
did not personally design, and that they can have a role in changing them.
Those ideas are not contradictory.
Personal guilt asks, what did I do?
Institutional responsibility asks, what am I participating in, and what can I influence?
We should not demand inherited guilt.
We can demand honesty about inherited conditions.
Second myth, anti-racism is reverse racism.
There is a legitimate principle underneath that concern.
People should not be treated unfairly because of race, whoever is affected.
Anti-racism does not give an employer permission to humiliate white employees, stereotype Asian
employees ignore Latino employees, or assume that any person of color has a single political
view.
And some DEI practices deserve criticism when they use racial essentialism, the idea that
people think or behave a certain way because of their race.
That is not a sophisticated analysis of power.
It is a stereotype with progressive packaging.
So we can defend racial equity while rejecting racial essentialism.
We can challenge unequal systems without assigning moral worth by category.
Third myth, DEI means lowering standards.
Good equity work should ask whether the standards are valid, job-related, and applied consistently.
That is not the same as abandoning standards.
The question is not, how do we let anyone in?
The question is, what is the job actually asking someone to do?
And what evidence predicts success?
A standard that is unrelated to performance is not rigorous.
It is decorative.
Another myth, if a policy is race neutral in its wording, it is automatically fair.
Neutral wording is relevant, but it is not the end of the analysis.
A rule can apply to everyone and still place heavier burdens on some groups.
That does not automatically make it unlawful or racist.
It does mean the institution should understand the effect and ask whether the burden is necessary.
A better sequence is, identify the pattern, test the data, examine possible causes, assess
legal and operational necessity, look for less burdensome alternatives, and monitor
the result.
Another myth, one training session can solve racism.
Research does not support that kind of promise.
A 2024 systematic review of DEI and anti-racism training studies found wide variation in content
and measures, few randomized designs, and a need to shift from one-time knowledge delivery
toward behavior and organizational change, longitudinal support, and rigorous evaluation.
That is a critique of weak training, not a reason to stop learning.
If a fire safety class does not make a building safe by itself, we do not conclude that
fire safety is a hoax.
We connect training to equipment, inspections, procedures, and accountability.
And we should be honest about what a training can do.
It can clarify expectations, teach a shared vocabulary, rehearse a response, or help
people recognize a pattern.
It cannot by itself rewrite a pay system, repair a broken complaint process, or change
who has decision authority.
And this one, if we treat everyone the same, we do not need equity work.
Treating people consistently is essential.
It is not always sufficient.
If a process is consistently difficult for people with limited English, consistently inaccessible
to people with disabilities, or consistently dependent on unpaid time and reliable transportation,
the institution should not call the result fair merely because the rule was applied consistently.
Equity is not a license for arbitrary exceptions.
It is a question about whether the design of the system allows eligible people a fair
chance to use it.
And that brings us to the most important distinction in the whole episode.
We can reject attacks that misrepresent DEI and still insist that DEI work meet a high
standard.
High standards for evidence, high standards for legality, high standards for dignity,
high standards for outcomes.
If a program cannot explain its purpose, measure its results, or show how it respects individuals,
it needs improvement.
If a public attack claims that any effort to reduce disparities is automatically discrimination,
that claim also needs improvement.
Let's sit with history for a moment, because there is a temptation to treat history as either
everything or nothing.
Right?
One version says history explains every current outcome, another says history is over, so
current outcomes can only reflect individual choices.
Both positions are too simple.
The answer is not to make every decision by race.
The answer is to use data responsibly enough to see whether the institution is meeting its
mission across the people it serves.
And they can reveal bigger design issues.
If a form is confusing, the problem may not be the form alone.
It may be a policy that asks for information the agency does not need, a data system
that cannot share records, or a culture that treats every mistake as evidence of
fraud.
This is why anti-racism in institutions is not mainly about adding a statement to a website.
It is about examining the chain from mission to rule to interaction to result.
And accepting that a person can be committed to fairness while still participating in
an unfair system, that is not an excuse.
It is a reason to look at systems as well as intentions.
Now let's bring that into the public sector directly.
Why is this especially important in government institutions?
Government is where the abstract questions become concrete.
If a private company makes a confusing form, that is frustrating.
If a public agency makes a confusing form, someone may lose food assistance, miss a deadline,
remain unsafe, or be unable to exercise a right.
And government often has a monopoly or near monopoly over the service.
People cannot simply switch to a different motor vehicle office, a different court,
a different benefits agency, or a different building inspector.
That power creates a special obligation.
Public institutions should be neutral in the sense of applying the law fairly.
But neutrality is not indifference to unequal access.
A government office can say, we apply the same rule to everyone and still need to ask
whether the rule is understandable, reachable, accessible, and necessary.
The Government Accountability Office has repeatedly connected good administration with goals, data,
performance measurement, and continuous improvement.
Those are not separate from equity.
They are the machinery that lets an agency discover whether its service is working for
the people it is meant to serve.
Consider a benefits program.
The formal eligibility rule may be clear, but the actual experience includes finding
the office, understanding the notice, gathering documents, getting childcare, taking time
off work, uploading files, correcting an error, and knowing what to do when the computer
rejects an application.
Each step has a burden, burdens accumulate, and they are not evenly distributed.
That difference is not necessarily proof of racial discrimination.
But if racial groups experience the burden differently, the agency should examine why.
Is geography part of it?
Language, disability, income, historic distrust, an automated identity check that works less
well for some documents, a rule that assumes a household structure that not everyone has.
And if the agency can reduce the burden without undermining program integrity, doing so is not
a favor.
It is better administration.
This is a theme we should keep repeating.
Equity is not a substitute for competence.
It is part of whether the institution is competent.
Because an agency that cannot tell who is failing to receive a service cannot claim
to be managing the service well.
So the public institution has a dual responsibility.
Comply with civil rights obligations and deliver the mission effectively.
Those goals should reinforce one another when the work is designed carefully.
The question for leaders is not just, do we have a DEI office?
It is, where in the operating system do we know whether people can access, participate
in and benefit from the institution?
That is a much more demanding question than checking a box.
It is also a more useful one.
Let's talk about what DEI can look like when it is done well.
I would start with a clear problem statement.
Yes.
Not we need more inclusion in the abstract, but our promotion process relies on informal
sponsorship and employees in some groups are receiving fewer opportunities.
Or residents who need interpretation abandon the application more often.
Or our complaint process is not trusted.
Then define the outcome.
What would improvement look like?
Shorter processing time, more complete applications, more consistent performance ratings, fewer preventable
appeals, better retention, a safer reporting climate.
Measurement can feel cold in a conversation about dignity, but without measurement the
institution may confuse activity with impact.
It can say, we held 12 trainings while not knowing whether managers handled complaints
more consistently.
Accountability does not mean a quota for every outcome.
It means giving someone responsibility for the agreed change, setting a review date
and explaining what happened.
And evaluation.
The institution should be willing to stop a program that is ineffective, revise one that
creates unintended harms and continue one that shows value.
What are some failure modes?
One is one-time training with no follow-up.
Another is a vague survey that measures whether people like the program, but not
whether the workplace changed.
Another is outsourcing responsibility to a single office while line managers continue to
control hiring assignments, discipline and promotion.
Another failure is treating lived experience as either infallible or irrelevant.
Experience is evidence of what happened to a person.
It may not by itself establish how often the pattern occurs or what caused it.
That is why it should be heard, documented, compared and connected to other evidence.
Another is using labels instead of decisions.
An agency can rename a committee, change a title or move a budget line and still leave
the underlying barriers untouched.
The work can focus on open access, transparent criteria, job-related standards,
barrier removal, accessibility, language access, consistent supervision and evidence-based improvement.
Those are not race-based preferences.
They are design and accountability choices.
There's a broader lesson here.
Effective DEI is less about saying the right words and more about building the right
feedback loops.
What was the goal?
Who was affected?
What did the data show?
What did people experience?
What changed?
What did we learn?
Those are questions any serious public institution should be able to answer.
We have talked about systems, but racism is also experienced emotionally.
People feel fear, humiliation, anger, exhaustion and sometimes disbelief.
A resident may know that a form is technically available and still feel that the institution
does not expect someone like them to succeed.
And employees can feel that too.
A person can be the first or only person of their background in a meeting, asked to
explain an entire community, interrupted, mistaken for someone else, or treated as evidence that
the organization is already inclusive.
There is a temptation to respond to those stories with a defensive intent.
That is not what we meant, but the person is describing what happened, not reading our
mind.
The right response is not to abandon due process or assume every allegation is proven.
It is to take the report seriously, protect people from retaliation, investigate fairly,
and correct the system if the evidence supports it.
That is the balance.
Believing that a concern deserves attention is not the same as prejudging every fact.
Backlash often grows when people feel that a change is being imposed without explanation,
or when they believe fairness has become a zero-sum contest.
Leaders should address that directly.
Explain the problem.
Explain the legal and operational boundaries.
Explain what is changing and what is not.
It also avoids using the most vulnerable employees as a shield.
An agency should not put one black employee, one native employee, one immigrant employee,
or one disability advocate in the position of defending every equity decision to everyone
else.
And people of color should not be expected to be endlessly patient teachers.
The institution must build its own capacity.
Defending the mission does not require defending every implementation.
The answer to both is the same habit.
Get concrete.
What happened?
Who was affected?
What does the evidence show?
What obligation does the institution have?
What is the least burdensome effect of change?
How will we know?
That is not always satisfying.
It is, however, how public institutions earn trust.
If someone listening works in government, what can they do on Monday morning?
Start with the service, not the slogan.
Choose one process that affects the public and map the actual experience from beginning
to end.
Where do people wait?
What do they have to understand?
What can go wrong?
Who has discretion?
Look at administrative burden.
Can the form be shorter?
Can the agency reuse information?
Can a resident get help in another language?
Can someone with a disability use the service without having to ask for a special exception?
Build accountability into ordinary management.
Put the action in the work plan.
Assign an owner, set a review date, ask for a result, not just an activity report.
And practice the language of repair.
If the agency made a mistake, say what it was.
If the policy is necessary, explain why.
If a change is not feasible now, describe the constraint and the next step.
For leaders, it means making equity part of performance and service quality, not assigning
it to the person with the word diversity in their title.
And for all of us, it means resisting the fantasy that we can become permanently innocent
by using the right language.
We will miss things, we will make mistakes.
The measure is whether we learn, repair, and change the pattern.
That is a demanding standard.
It is also a humane one.
Because it does not ask anyone to be perfect.
It asks institutions to be accountable.
So what is anti-racism?
It is not a claim that every white person is bad.
It is not permission to stereotype.
It is not a substitute for evidence, legality, competence, or individual dignity.
It is the practice of looking honestly at how racial inequity can be produced, including
through ordinary systems and then changing what can be changed.
It means taking intent seriously without hiding behind it.
It means treating disparities as questions to investigate, not verdicts to announce
or ignore.
And in public institutions, it means remembering that fairness is part of performance.
The public does not experience our mission statement.
People experience the form, the call, the weight, the decision, and the way they are
treated.
The work is not finished by a training, a committee, or a new acronym.
It is built through thousands of choices.
Clearer rules, better data, accessible services, consistent standards, honest accountability,
and the willingness to repair what is not working.
That work can be uncomfortable.
It can also be ordinary.
An ordinary, sustained institutional practice is where lasting change usually begins.
Thanks for listening.
